posts.title: Researchers asked parents how they would feel about an AI leading their child's therapy session. Three in four were not comfortable.
posts.researchVerificationStatus: VERIFIED, verdict EDIT (reviewed before the ten checks were required)

linkedin.text:
A survey in JAMA Pediatrics asked parents in the United States how comfortable they would be with an AI leading a behavioural therapy session for their child. About three in four were not.

Of the 572 parents who answered, 47.2 percent were not comfortable at all and 28.8 percent were not too comfortable.

The headline version would be that parents do not trust AI with children. The study does not say that.

It asked one hypothetical question about AI led behavioural therapy, in an opt in sample, and it measured stated comfort, not what parents would choose in practice, whether the therapy was effective, or whether it helped or harmed a child. The children, aged 5 to 17, were not asked. Neither were parents in the UK.

Everyday use of AI by parents and children made no difference to comfort. That cuts against the easy explanation that people fear what is unfamiliar.

This looks more like a judgement about where AI belongs.

I build a parent tool with an AI guide in it, so I am not neutral. The boundary matters. Guidance that helps a parent think through a situation is not therapy delivered to a child. Our stage check is three questions about one child, and it is the parent who answers them. Nothing we make diagnoses or treats, and a serious worry belongs with a professional.

The survey also asked what would matter most, and 546 parents answered. They could choose more than one. Accuracy of diagnosis was chosen by 58.5 percent, empathy by 49.4 percent, recommendation from a medical professional by 46.8 percent, and confidentiality and privacy by 43.7 percent.

That list is more useful than a broad argument about whether AI is good or bad. Before a child uses an AI tool for something that matters, ask what it is for, who oversees it, and where what the child says goes.

The source is in the comments.

If more parents and school leaders need a clearer line between guidance and treatment, repost this. The boundary should be visible before trust is requested.

When an AI tool is offered for a child's wellbeing, what would you need to see before you trusted the boundary it claims to keep?

posts.title: Researchers ran 32,555 pretend conversations between teenagers and AI chatbots. When the teen pushed back, the safety slipped.
posts.researchVerificationStatus: VERIFIED, verdict EDIT (reviewed before the ten checks were required)

linkedin.text:
A preprint on arXiv put 18 chatbot models through 32,555 simulated conversations with teenagers. Telling each model it was talking to a teenager cut the criterion failure rate from 43.3 percent to 24.9 percent.

Good news. Half of it.

None of these were real teenagers, and none of them were the apps children actually download. The researchers wrote 106 scenarios from clinical cases, turned them into 983 versions, and had an AI judge score every reply against 22 safety checks.

The scoring was strict: a chatbot failed a check in a scenario if it failed in any single version of that conversation, which means 43.3 percent is not the share of conversations that went wrong, and it says nothing about how often a real child is harmed.

The part I keep coming back to is what happened when the simulated teenager pushed back.

Without the teen aware instruction, failures around diagnosis, medication and substances rose by about 10 to 12 percentage points for more than 80 percent of the chatbots once the teenager said no.

A boundary held at the first answer. Then it slipped.

It is a preprint. It tested models through developer connections, not consumer apps with their own safety layers. It cannot tell us that any particular app is unsafe, and it does not show that children should be kept away from AI.

What it does give a parent is a question worth practising at the kitchen table.

Ask your child what they would do if a chatbot told them not to worry about something that worried you. Then ask what they would do if it kept agreeing after they said they did not want to tell anyone.

Our schools lesson on AI companions is built around one question: "It talks like it knows me. Does it?" I also build a parent tool with an AI guide in it, and that guide talks to the parent. It is never a chat partner for the child.

The source is in the comments.

If a parent or teacher you know needs this, repost it. An AI can be useful and still be the wrong thing to trust with a hard decision.

What phrase would you teach a child to use when an AI starts sounding like a friend taking sides?

posts.title: Ask 13 and 14 year olds how they protect themselves online and about a third say they talk to an adult. By 17 and 18 it is fewer than one in five.
posts.researchVerificationStatus: VERIFIED, verdict EDIT (reviewed before the ten checks were required)

linkedin.text:
The number that stayed with me was 18 percent.

The European Commission asked 26,297 young people aged 13 to 18 across the 27 EU countries what they do to protect their mental wellbeing on social media. The survey ran from 30 March to 16 April 2026.

Among young people who use social media on a school day, 32 percent of those aged 13 and 14 chose talking to a parent, teacher or another adult. At 15 and 16 it was 28 percent. At 17 and 18 it was 18 percent.

That does not mean teenagers stop talking to their parents as they grow. These were three different age groups surveyed at one point, not the same children followed over time. The answer also grouped parents, teachers and other adults together. The UK was not included.

There is another part of the picture. The older group more often chose reporting harmful content or accounts and taking breaks from social media. They may be developing other ways to manage what they meet online.

Even so, the gap matters. Older teenagers in the same survey more often reported seeing AI content that was hard to recognise and unwanted sexualised content, while fewer named an adult as one of the ways they protect themselves.

It makes me think about timing. The open door is easier to build in an ordinary calm moment than when something has already gone wrong.

I build a parent tool, and one of its first lessons gives parents a simple line: if a screen ever gives you that uh oh feeling, you can always come to me. You will never be in trouble for telling me.

The research does not show that saying this changes what a teenager will do years later. It is simply a useful promise a parent can make now.

Could you say that sentence tonight, while nothing is wrong?

posts.title: Young people handed researchers their real TikTok feeds. Almost all the news and politics in them came from accounts they did not follow.
posts.researchVerificationStatus: VERIFIED, verdict EDIT (reviewed before the ten checks were required)

linkedin.text:
Parents often ask who their child follows.

A new study suggests that may be the wrong first question.

Researchers asked 147 young people in the Netherlands, aged 16 to 25, to donate their real TikTok feed histories. Together those histories covered about 6.7 million public videos, mostly from October 2023 to May 2026.

For the typical person in the study, news, politics and societal issues made up 5.34 percent of the feed, or about 126 videos a month.

The striking part was where that content came from. A median of 98.4 percent came from accounts the person did not follow, based on the accounts they followed when they donated their data.

That does not mean 98.4 percent of every young person's feed came from strangers. The figure describes the median person in a small volunteer sample. Some participants saw much less from unfollowed accounts. These were older teenagers and young adults in one country, not children in the UK. The paper is a preprint, and it does not show any effect on beliefs, mood, politics or wellbeing.

But it does expose a useful gap in the usual family conversation.

We tend to ask, who do you follow? The feed has another question built into it: why did the system choose to show you this?

That distinction belongs in preparation before a child has to work it out alone. In the Guided Childhood primary curriculum, a lesson on how algorithms work gives children a simple starting point: you do not choose the feed, the algorithm does.

The study does not prove that this lesson changes what a child later sees or believes. It supports the practical reason for teaching how recommendation systems work before the feed becomes ordinary.

When you next look at a feed together, could you ask: why do you think it showed you this?
